I do have a tip for new people: Spend an evening learning the keyboard shortcuts for switching between the tools. It'll only take you a few hours to master them and will save you tons of time in the long run.

Aseprite is 100% catered towards pixel art, and just that. You will never get features that slow your system down or ones that make the pixel art creation harder or un-fun for no reason.

If you have around $20 bucks to spare, don't hesitate to pick this up.

To keep this review brief, it is clear how this application has become something of an industry go-to/standard for pixel artists and game makers who use pixelated styles.

The interface is simplistic and easy to learn without compromising on effectiveness, intuitive even if you're using a mouse or trackpad instead of a drawing tablet, and has keyboard shortcuts for some uncommon tools I wish were more readily available in my other art applications.

My favourite shortcuts are:
- Shift+R; which allows you to select a colour from your image, and replace any instance of that colour on that frame (or, alternatively, wherever you have selected/lassoed and across multiple layers and/or frames in animations), with whatever colour you like. This is especially handy when animating videogame sprites, because needing to change, for example, a character's shirt colour, can be as easy as highlighting those layers and frames, and replacing them all in the span of two button presses and five clicks, as apposed to having to recolour the frames by hand, one by one.
- Shift+O; This outlines whatever you have drawn. You can pick what "faces" of the image recieve the outline, how thick the outline is, whether it extends inwards or outwards, and what colour it is. It can be quite handy, and a good time saver.
- Ctrl+Shift+I (the letter i, not the letter L); this inverts your active selection. It's convenient when you're having to work inside sprites, as Aseprite currently does not have a clipping mask feature.
- Ctrl+Shift+C; instead of copying from within your selection/lasso on *just the active/selected layer*, this copies *all visible pixels* within your selection - particularly helpful if you want to be able to quickly frankenstein your sprite to test ideas.
- And of course the classic Ctrl+Z (undo) and Shift+Ctrl+Z (redo), as well as Ctrl+C (copy) and Ctrl+V (paste).

There are other shortcuts, but those are the ones I use most often.

Another tool I use is the grid; helpful for tilesets and spritesheets. You can set your grid size by making a selection on your canvas, and while that area is selected, go to the bar at the top of the application, and click View>Grid>Selection as Grid.

There are also different colour settings for your files. It can be hard to wrap your head around "Indexed" works, but when you get it, it's pretty much a constantly active "colour replace" tool, where if you alter the colours in your pallete, it changes the occurances of that colour in your artwork to match. This gets complicated in images with lots of colours, but for sprites that have limited palletes, it saves time when testing different colours and shading intensities.

The animation feature has a customisable onion-skin tool; it does the job well. You can choose the opacity for the onion skins, whether they're tinted to show which frame is before or after the selected one, and whether it appear behind or in front of your current frame. You can also choose whether its showing everything that is visible in the next/previous frame, or just what is on the specific layer you have selected.

The animations also have a tagging feature, which is VERY helpful when creating character/unit sprites that have multiple animations you'd like to keep on-model.

There are lots of exporting modes you can use; there's the obvious ability to save things as an aseprite file, but you can export your files as MANY file types (I predominantly use PNGs and Gifs). If your work has multiple frames, you can choose whether you're exporting every frame, just the frames you have currently selected, or frames within a specific tag name. You can do the same for layers, too. You can also choose what scale you're exporting these files at (for example, if you're making a character that is 10x20 pixels, you can export it at its normal 100% scaling for the game, but 500% (5X) for if you wanted to share it with your dev-team, social media, and/or friends in a way where they can actually see it without them having to zoom in or risk their device making it blurry in its attempts to up-scale it.

Another notable export mode is "Export Sprite Sheet", which takes all of the seperate frames of your animation, and turns it into a single framed, layed out sprite sheet you can import into your gamebuilding software (Eg, Unity).

Worth mentioning, Aseprite does also have modes for the layers (the classic ones such as overlay, colour burn, difference, saturation, colour, etc), and you can change your layer names and opacities. That is likely assumed as a given, but just in case anyone wasn't sure, I can confirm those are things it has.

The only downside that comes to mind, is that Aseprite does not have a clipping mask feature; as I mentioned in the keyboard shortcuts section moment ago. The easiest (but still effective) way to circumnavigate this, is by using the magic wand select tool to select the empty space on the layer you want to clipping mask, inverting that selection so that you have only the filled-in areas selected, and then select the layer you want to treat as the "clipping mask" layer. You should still have that selection, which effectively means you cannot draw outside of the filled-in areas. So, in short, it doesn't technically have a clipping mask tool, but you can rig something that works like one in 30-60 seconds.

If you want to clipping mask a folder of layers, or your whole image, you can do that by having only those parts of the image visible, then highlighting your whole asset and pressing Ctrl+Shift+C, which will copy all visible pixels. You can then use Ctrl+V to paste that image onto your "clipping mask" layer, magic wand to select the empty space around it, and then using Ctrl+Shift+I (again, this is i, not L) to invert the selection. From there, you can use your eraser to get rid of the image you've copied, but retain the selected outline. It can get annoying if you need to return to this clipping mask, but if it's one you have to return to often, you can have a layer you keep invisible most of the time where you can keep that pasted copy, so you can turn it on and get the selection, then turn it back off and move to your clipping mask layer while it's still active. 

I use this application for work, to create character sprites (dialogue portraits and animated units), videogame environment assets and buildings (predominantly following a top-down tiling perspective), and larger drawn scenes for videogame capsule art and concept images.

I realise I didn't actually keep this as brief as I had intended, haha. I digress; I like this application a lot, and with the amount of time I've spent using it, it's more than earned the time it took me to write this. I highly recommend it. It's more than worth the price (especially considering how hard it is to get one-time-purchase, high-quality drawing applications these days). I will likely continue using this application for many years.

some tips to try if you are new: 

- you can select a whole section of cells (click and drag) and copy that section ( ctrl + C ) and then paste (ctrl + v) it into a set of new cells or override other ones so that way if you have a recurring animation you can easily repeat it without redoing it or copy and pasting 1 by 1
- It is a lot easier on your memory and when exporting if you are exporting something at its exact size if it is small, or if it is something big, then make it small but export it by say 200%
- If you are doing something for streaming or what something to go by typical screen size, I found exporting it at 1080 x 1920 is like, the most my own personal computer can handle, but you can also create your work at 400% less that size (270 x 480) and export it by 400%
- When you use the fill tool, to get more colors filled at a time instead of using the bucket pixel by pixel, there is a button at the top after you select the paint bucket that lets you fill by 8 points instead of 4 (SUPER HELPFUL)
- You can import color palettes by opening the color palette section and clicking and dragging a photo in that has the colors you want in it
- You can type in your own hex codes and rgb color codes when trying to get an exact color
- UTILIZE THE SHORTCUTS! Alt + D is so handy when trying to duplicate layers, check out the others too when trying to select tools
- be careful that when you are selecting a certain part of your image, if you are trying to copy and paste the selection, make sure you are only doing it for the selection -- there were many times I accidently copy and pasted a whole cell or even accidentally deleted it
- when making selections, clear selection (ctrl + D I think?) before switching layers because sometimes it would completely cut the selection from the layer if you werent intending to

for context, i've been an indie game developer for around 20 years, and have used a lot of programs to create pixel art in that time. i'm primarily a programmer but have spent a lot of time doing the pixel art for my games as well. i've made over 14 games, most using pixel art, all 2D. the programs i've used to make pixel art have been paint shop pro, neopaint, photoshop, gimp, mario paint (which was the first one i ever made pixel art in, as a kid playing around with it on the snes), in-built pixel art tools in the ohrrpgce and game maker engines, and many others.
